reason: NASA completely forgot about its lunar trees until an email from an elementary school teacher forced a planetary scientist to hunt them down.
story: In 1971, Apollo 14 astronaut Stuart Roosa carried hundreds of tree seeds in his personal kit while orbiting the Moon. This joint NASA and Forest Service project aimed to study how space travel affected plant life. Back on Earth, the seed canister accidentally burst inside a decontamination vacuum chamber, but the Forest Service successfully germinated them anyway. In 1975 and 1976, hundreds of these Moon trees were planted across the U.S. for the bicentennial, but NASA kept no records of their locations. By 1996, the trees were completely forgotten. That year, third-grade teacher Joan Goble and her class found a sycamore labeled Moon tree at an Indiana camp. When Goble emailed NASA, archivist Dave Williams and his colleagues had no idea what she was talking about. Williams dug through old archives, built a public tracking website, and sparked a nationwide hunt that continues to find these long-lost space monuments.
angle: NASA completely forgot about hundreds of Moon trees grown from space-travelled seeds until a third-grade class randomly found one in 1996.

claims.claim: Stuart Roosa, a former Forest Service smokejumper, served as the Command Module Pilot on NASA's Apollo 14 mission in 1971.
Roosa carried hundreds of tree seeds inside his personal kit while orbiting the Moon.
The seed experiment was a joint project between NASA and the U.S. Forest Service.
The seeds were chosen from five species: loblolly pine, sycamore, sweetgum, redwood, and Douglas fir.
After returning to Earth, the seed bags accidentally burst inside a decontamination vacuum chamber.
Despite the accident, the Forest Service successfully germinated the seeds into hundreds of viable seedlings.
Many of the saplings were distributed and planted in 1975 and 1976 to celebrate the U.S. bicentennial.
Several Moon trees were planted in foreign countries, including Brazil, Switzerland, and Japan.
After over forty years, there was no discernible difference between the Moon trees and their Earth-bound counterparts.
A loblolly pine Moon tree was planted at the White House but later died.
NASA failed to keep any official records or track the planting locations of the Moon trees.
In 1996, a third-grade teacher named Joan Goble and her students found a Moon tree in Indiana.
Goble emailed NASA planetary scientist Dave Williams, who was completely unaware that Moon trees existed.
Most of Williams's colleagues at NASA were also completely unaware of the trees.
Williams researched the history, found old newspaper clippings, and posted a NASA webpage asking the public for help finding the trees.
Williams established a database to track verified Moon trees based on reports from the public.
Stuart Roosa's daughter, Rosemary Roosa, continues his legacy by helping run a foundation that plants second-generation Moon trees.
NASA revived the program in 2022 by flying more than 1,000 seeds around the Moon on Artemis I.

disputed: The exact number of seeds Roosa carried is disputed, with sources claiming either about 500 or more than 2,000 seeds; a script should refer generally to 'hundreds of seeds' to avoid contradiction.

The details about an initial, failed germination attempt in Houston due to inadequate facilities are only mentioned in S2, while other sources only mention successful germination at Forest Service stations; a script should focus on the successful germination at the Forest Service stations.
